whisper.text:
Hello everyone, this is Frank DeFreitas and we have a very special guest in the studio with us today, Michelle Roy. How are you, Michelle? I'm good, Frank. How about you? I want to thank you for coming out on such a cold day, 25 degrees below zero wind chill. I know, not good, not good. You don't live far from me. I could have done this with you on the phone, so I appreciate you coming in. Because I like to do these live in the studio and very rarely do I ever have the chance because there are so many people in holography which are scattered not only across the country but around the globe. It's just impossible to have people come into the studio, but it's nice to have you here. It's good to be here. Before we get started, I would just like to tell the listeners a little bit about my impressions with Michelle Roy and why I'm so excited about the show this week. I got involved with the Freelance Group for Career and Workforce Innovation probably about a year and a half to two years ago through my involvement with Lehigh University and a startup science museum. It's called the Discovery Center of Science and Technology. Bill Freed, who is the president and CEO of the Freelance Group, was also at the Discovery Center working on workforce development. I was there setting up their laser and holography programs, laser light shows. I would do demonstrations for the public where they would come in and see the laser light show, but because it was an educational institution, I would go over all the different things that lasers were capable of and what holograms were capable of. But I would also always tie in how lasers are used in industry, in science, technology, art, etc. Bill and I began to speak, and I learned that basically what he does, and Michelle, you'll be able to clarify this or take it a step further, is the bottom line for the Freelance Group is the fact that the end result is to be able to have people go into the workforce and be matched. They're matched closely with their interests and what it is that they need to do. And Michelle, you can tell us a little bit more about that. But Michelle is also involved with the Freelance Group, and now what we're doing is beginning to put programs together for lasers and holography where I go out and do my normal presentation of what lasers are about and what holograms are, but the Freelance Group, and specifically Michelle Roy, who's going to be working with me, is going to give people information and guide them along the path of, you know, moving into the field of photonics. So this is a very good thing. And Michelle is a very special person since I've had a chance to meet her, and I'm very happy that she's on the show, and I'm extremely happy that they're going to be involved with lasers and holography due to the fact that, number one, she's a very, very intelligent person. But combine that with the fact that she's also sharp, which if any of you get emails from Dr. So-and-so or Dr. So-and-so, and you read those emails, you think how does this person even get dressed in the morning and go out, you know, to perform anything. Michelle, on the other hand, combines that intelligence with... The ability to get dressed in the morning. Yeah. And also the level of professionalism that she has, and she's also very highly polished with her presentation skills. So this is very good for the field of holography, and I'm very honored to not only just have her in the studio, but to be able to bring this program to you, but also the fact that she's going to be working to get people involved out there in the industry with lasers and photonics, and two of those things that are happening quickly. Monday night, January 24th at 7.30 at Georgian Court College in Lakewood, New Jersey, we're going to be doing a presentation for the public on lasers and holography in the Arts and Science Center. And also another one on May 6th at the Smithsonian Institute in Washington, D.C., at the Rishon Museum. We will be doing a very similar thing throughout the day, and Bill Freed will also be down there where you can meet Bill Freed as well. And I'm sure we'll have Bill Freed on the show at some point. He's down in Florida right now while we freeze our butts off up here in Allentown. So Bill, if you're listening to this... We're not happy. We're not happy, yeah. So Michelle, why don't we start off... Why don't you tell us a little bit about yourself and also a little bit about FreedLance. Okay. Well, as you mentioned at the beginning, I work with FreedLance, and our work is in the field of career development. We do that in a variety of ways, working with organizations and agencies to help them provide better career development services to people. I guess probably I should start by sort of defining the whole idea of career development. Yeah, which most people don't even think about. Right. I mean, if you're going to go out and buy a stereo, you have all of these books and magazines that you're looking at to find out what the frequency response is, how many watchable speakers handle, what all that. But when you go out for a job, you have nothing. Right. Yeah. I think about when I first got a job, my first job out of college was as an admissions counselor at a junior college. Which is a great thing.

you have nothing. Right. Yeah. I think about when I first got a job, my first job out of college was as an admissions counselor at a junior college, which I just fell into that. I had no plans for what I was going to do. I hadn't thought about, you know, what are my interests or abilities or where do I want to go. Actually, I think I just didn't want to leave school, so that was a way to, you know, get paid for staying in school. And so I just sort of fell into that job. And I think a lot of people do that. So the idea of career development really is that you've thought about what your interests and abilities are, the things that you're good at, done some research on careers that are out there and so forth. And I'll get more into that in a little detail later on, I think. But just this idea that you think about your career as something that you would put more time and effort and research into than the same amount of time and effort and research as you would put into researching a stereo system, or at least or maybe even more. But a lot of people don't know how to do that. They're not, they don't understand what resources are out there. They don't do a lot of planning around their careers. They don't even think of themselves as having careers. They think of it as just, you know, a job, just how I pay the bills. So the FreedLance group is really interested in helping people get into careers where there's a definite career path. You've thought about what you want to do and how you want to do that to make you happier. Because really the bottom line is if we're not happy with the work that we do, then we tend to not do a very good job. We tend to not do a very good job with it. And we tend to not maybe be able to progress the ways that we would like to because we're just not into it. So the FreedLance group, that's basically what we do is work with, you know, individuals and agencies and so forth to educate them about the career development process and, you know, how to effectively look for careers. My background actually, I mentioned my first job was in higher education. So I'm familiar with the higher education arena and what kinds of college majors and majors are out there and that kind of thing. I then went from that into human resources where I was a human resources manager for a couple of companies in the Lehigh Valley. So I know the kinds of things that employers are looking for and how that whole, how to recruit, you know, when I get a resume and, you know, what kinds of things do we look at, what do we look for in interviews and so forth. And then I actually worked for a local organization, a nonprofit that was involved in career development and providing career development services to clients. Thank you. And then I also worked for a local organization that was involved in career development services and providing career development services to clients. And so I, you know, got a hold of that piece of the picture. So really my background has been in a lot of different areas and now I have the opportunity to really piece those different areas together to help people in, you know, identifying careers and moving forward in their careers. What is a job exactly? I know that, I imagine through the U.S. Department of Labor they have different codes and everything, whether you happen to be a person that washes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. microbiologist, there's a category and a code for that specific job. And I don't know if O-Net is the correct thing for that. Right. Well, O-Net is a way of looking at jobs. Previously, they've had what they called the O-O-H, the Occupational Outlook Handbook. And that was primarily based on, well, they have different categories of jobs. You know, science and technology, for example, would be a category, and then there would be specific jobs within that category. And the O-O-H, the Occupational Outlook Handbook, was an annual publication that the Department of Labor put out that has descriptions of various jobs. Excuse me. It wasn't based on skills. What we're finding now, and you bring up the concept of O-Net, O-Net is a new way of looking at jobs that the Department of Labor has come up with that's based on skills and what people know how to do as opposed to a specific job description. Because I think what we're finding more and more is that we're not going, we're not going into specific jobs necessarily. We're using constellations of skills in different ways. Yes, there are specific names for jobs and specific occupations, obviously, but the most effective way for people to be able to look for work or to think about what careers to prepare for is thinking about it in terms of what their skills and interests are. And so the O-Net way of looking at work is designed to help job seekers or students or whoever think about jobs. So in terms of this would be a good job for me because of my interests and abilities. This would be a good job for me because of my work values, for example, which I can get in, I'll get into that in a little bit more detail later on. So, you know, that's basically, it's sort of a paradigm shift, you know, a different way of looking at it. Do you know if holography is listed with any of these things as an actual job? Because there are professional holographers, obviously. It is an industry that is growing. Right. There are companies that are providing professional services. Yes. Yes. There are companies that are providing services in creating three-dimensional laser holograms. But I think through some of the experiences that I've had looking, I have never seen holography ever mentioned.

services in creating three-dimensional laser holograms. But I think through some of the experiences that I've had looking, I have never seen holography ever mentioned as a job. Right. Not to my knowledge. Is there any, you know, I have never seen, I agree with you. You know, I've done a lot of research, too, and, you know, in the Occupational Outlook handbook, we never had holographer. I know that in the O-Net database, there's no such thing as holographer. Part of the problem with that, or part of the reason for that, I guess I should say, is that government moves very slowly. And let us not forget that the Department of Labor, who publishes books like, you know, or has O-Net and Occupational Outlook handbook, they are not necessarily as on top of emerging careers, which holography is definitely anything in lasers and photonics. That's what we would call an emerging career. They're not as good about getting that information. So you can have tons. You can have tons of stuff on, you know, how to be a secretary, you know, clerical work. But they're not as good at coming up with emerging careers. As an example, I have not seen anything on Webmaster or anything in web design. Now, that's been around for a number of years as well. I mean, relatively speaking, it's been around for several years. And there really is nothing about that in there. I think that they have some difficulty getting their hands around those sometimes. Now, the people who are out there right now, the holotalkers, the public listeners that are listening to this program, I guess since the government does this, we'll do this for this show. We're going to break them down into categories. And I would say that the majority of people would fall into probably three categories. We would have the students who log on at a very heavy rate right now because science fair time is coming up. And a lot of schools pass out assignments to, you know, look into lasers and holography. So there's a lot of listeners that are students. There are a lot of teachers. There are a lot of teachers which follow what's happening with the field, basically science teachers. But you'll find some art teachers in there as well. And then there are the holographers themselves, which is category three, which we could break down into subcategories of professional holographers who get their income, you know, from doing holography. And your amateur and hobbyist holographer who has probably been doing holography for years but does it as a sideline, you know, to their normal job that they go to each day. So why don't we start off by, you know, examining those categories of listeners and then talk about how they would fit into moving on if they were interested in doing so ever to having a career in lasers and holography. So why don't we start with the students? Okay. In understanding career development, Frank, there are stages that people go through in their careers. And so, for example, when we're talking about students, and I know that you have listeners who are, you know, probably maybe a few in elementary school. But, you know, middle school, high school, college, and so forth, there are different stages of looking at careers because of their ages. I mean, obviously, a sixth grader is not going to be looking for a job next year. So they have different issues compared to a college senior who obviously will be looking for a job at some point. So there's that whole, there are different stages that we're looking at. I think following through, you know, starting with younger listeners and moving on all the way up, the first stage of looking at careers is what we call the career exploration stage. And that's where you're just really starting to be aware of what jobs are out there. You're starting to be more aware of yourself. What are the things that I'm interested in doing? Where do I show talent? What kinds of abilities do I have and so forth? You're just kind of feeling your way around, seeing what's available, thinking about how do you fit in with different things. Now, the interesting thing, I think, for students, and thinking about this, and I think this is a really important thing, is that you're not just thinking about, you know, thinking about middle school as an example. Lots of people think, well, middle school is way too early to be thinking about careers. You know, I mean, they're kids. You know, that's way too early. It's not, though, because people make decisions starting in middle school about the courses that they're going to take in high school that then might prepare them for college courses. If they don't take, you know, certain math or science courses starting in middle school, they're not going to be able to take the courses they need to take in high school that, you know, then they would need to take. Right. They might not be able to take in college. So now is a good time to be thinking, you know, in middle school is a good time to start thinking about that stuff, just so you're sure that you have the foundations educationally for what you may want to do in the future. So at the middle school level, we're really talking about exploration, starting to really feel, feel out what kinds of jobs are out there beyond, you know, I know my dad does this or my mom does that, and thinking about, you know, the possibility that they want to go on for higher education and being prepared, you know, by taking that course. And so that's what we're talking about. We're talking about taking the appropriate courses. High school starts to be a little more targeted obviously, because students are starting to make some decisions about, do I want to go to college? Do I want to get a job right out of school? I will say this. Everything that I've seen about. Two. Two. Two. Two. Two. Two. Two. Two. Two. Two. Two. Two. Two. Two. Two. Two. Two. Two. Two.

because students are starting to make some decisions about, do I want to go to college, do I want to get a job right out of school? I will say this, everything that I've seen about two things. One, everything that I've seen about wanting to be successful or being able to make a lot of money, as an example, which is what a lot of people want to do and be able to find jobs, you need some level of higher education for most jobs. I've seen stats that say 80% of jobs are going to require some type of post-secondary that's after high school. Kind of training or education. That doesn't necessarily mean a four-year degree or a master's or a Ph.D. It could be a one-year certificate or a two-year degree. Technical training. Exactly. But you need something beyond high school at this stage of the game. So that, again, they're starting to be aware of, okay, well, I want to meet, I'm going to go to college or I want to major in this. So you start to become more targeted about the jobs that you're considering and the interest areas that you want to go into. And exploring those options and making plans for getting into those options. Once you say someone goes to college, then obviously career development then becomes a lot about taking the right courses and finding a job. And I have some leads or some resources that people could access in terms of jobs and lasers and photonics. But there, that's when you're starting to really get at specific employers that you might want to work for and that kind of thing. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Then it turns more into like job search. Now, once you're out there, and that's what leads us, of course, to the holographers who have already graduated or, you know, whatever, who are out there, there's that whole concept of moving along in your career. And so you need to be aware of, you know, well, here's where I am right now in this job. Where do I want to be? What do I want to do? What skills do I need to take me there? What training, what experiences do I need? And starting to get into those, make sure that you're, you know, doing continuing education, you're reading a lot, you know, all of those things to upgrade your skills so you can move along on a career path. Some people are happy, you know, I'll just stay in this one job and I'm fine with that. But, you know, many people want to try different things. And it doesn't necessarily mean climbing a ladder, you know, where you're getting promotions. It could be trying out different, you know, well, I have been in this kind of job, but now I'm going to make a lateral move, which is essentially the same level, over to something different that lets me try out some different, you know, experiences or learn some new skills or whatever. Now, when we get into the area of teachers and educators, as you're aware, the state of Florida just adopted holography as part of the standards. How should teachers start to think? Should they be thinking at all about that, hey, not only am I teaching about lasers and holography, but kids could do this as a career as well? Oh, absolutely. Is that something that they're thinking about? Absolutely. Do teachers need to think about it at all? Absolutely. A couple of things about that. One is I know that there are a lot of states, and I don't know if Florida is one of these or not, who as part of their state standards, they have what we call workforce readiness standards, which means that they are supposed to be infusing career development activities into the curriculum, exposing kids to career options, helping them identify their interests and abilities and so forth. So that, for many states, is part of what they have to do in order for a kid to be able to graduate. But the other part of it is that part of the educational process is preparing kids for success when they leave high school. And obviously when we all leave school, at some point we have to get a job. And so helping kids understand early on and all the way through the process how career development works, how their interests and abilities might fit in with various jobs that are out there, what their work values are, all of those things really needs to be part of what teachers are doing in the classroom. They're facilitating, if you will, the career development of students. So they need to be exposing kids to different options. Constantly, because my husband was a teacher, you know, he's a principal, and he used to laugh about, you know, kids would say, well, why do I have to know this anyway? You know, what's important? You know, how is this relevant to me? And I think most of us ask that, you know, when we're in an educational setting. And one of the ways to make, you know, class and things relevant is by showing kids how this ties into various career options. And, hey, you really like doing this? Guess what? You could do this for a living. I should have said this at the beginning. There's an excellent book. It's called Do What You Love and the Money Will Follow. To me, the number one rule of career development is for you to find out what it is you love to do. What do you have a passion about? What makes you want to get up and keep moving in the morning? What engages? What engages you? And when you're doing work that you really love, then the money will follow. And I think you know that, too, in your career, Frank. There's no sense in people going out and doing jobs. It's not about the money.

you. And when you're doing work that you really love, then the money will follow. And I think you know that too in your career, Frank. There's no sense in people going out and doing jobs that they hate. It's just not productive in your life. It's not productive in any aspect. People who hate their jobs are really unhappy. So students need to be thinking about, you know, what is it I really love to do? How can I get a job in that? How can I turn that into something I get paid for? And those are the people who are really successful. I mean, Bill Gates, who I know is not necessarily a favorite of yours, but you know, there's a guy who really loves what he does. And his passion led him to great success. That's obviously on a larger, more famous scale. But frankly, I love what I do. And so I consider myself successful. You know, I don't have Bill Gates's money, but I love what I do. And I'm successful because I love what I do. So I think that that's really successful. And so I think that's really successful. You know, I don't have Bill Gates's money, but I love what I do. And so I consider myself successful. You know, I don't have a moral responsibility almost that teachers have, an ethical responsibility to help kids tap into what is it that you love? What is your passion? Let's look at how we could turn this into something really great for you when you leave, because that is what will guarantee your success. So, all right, that's my setback. Okay. Very interesting stuff. And what I love about what I do is the fact that when you call me in the middle of July, I have a nice holder on the raft that I float on the pool. That's right. So if you call me, chances are I will pick that up while I'm floating in the pool and talk to you. So that's something I love very much about what I do. Yeah. See, I need to get to the pool level. I'm not there yet. Now, there's another sphere of people involved with holography. And as far as people who are involved with holography, it's probably the largest sphere. And even more so than people who are working professionally in the field are the amateur and hobbyist holographers who would just absolutely love to be able to do that. So, what would you say to people who are doing that? Well, there's a lot of people who would love to be able to do this on a regular basis. If someone, let's say John Doe or Jane Doe out in the state of Minnesota has a holography lab in their basement and they feel like they've been working with lasers and holograms, understands the concepts very well, and they decided that they wanted to somehow move into working with this thing professionally, what about them? A few things in regard to that. And let me take it back a step if I could. Obviously, someone who's in their basement doing holography, loving it, has already started to think about what interests they have and what abilities they have that could be related to a career. And that's really the first step of career development. We call that, you know, know yourself, know who you are. So, obviously, that person has figured out who they are and that this is something that they really want to do. Once you know that and you've narrowed it down to... ...some occupational areas, which obviously that person would have done, then you need to do some research and get some information. One of the things that I would...and it depends on how targeted the person wants to be. There are lots of jobs in, you know, using lasers and photonics. It can be in, you know, a manufacturing or industrial setting. Oh, okay. You could be an artist using holography or, you know, using lasers. You could be involved in... You could teach it. You know, there are lots of different ways you can use that talent or that skill. So, one of the things a person would need to do is kind of think about, well, what setting might I want to work in? How would I want to use this skill? I know, you know, someone who's probably moving in more of an artistic direction would be less interested in going to work for some manufacturer. So, that would be part of that thought process. What setting might I want to work in? Then they would need to do some research. And there are different ways to research occupations. I have a lot of resources on the web that people could go to to find out about careers you can...in lasers and photonics. One of the ways to do that would be to look at actual job openings and sort of get a sense for what are the job descriptions? You know, what kinds of things are people doing in these jobs? So that that could help them target, you know, what industry or what area of lasers. They might want to go into. Another one, and frankly, I think this is probably the most valuable way to do it, is to talk to people in the field. Talk to people who are actually in those jobs, who actually do the thing that you think you're interested in. And find out from them, you know, how did you get here? What kind of, you know, job experiences did you have prior to coming into this position? What education and training did you have? What advice do you have for me? You know, I'm interested in this. I'm interested in this career. What do I need to have? What do I need to know in order to get into this occupation? What do I need to be good at this occupation? What do you really do? Because another...

What do I need to have? What do I need to know in order to get into this occupation? What do I need to be good at this occupation? What do you really do? Because another thing I'm saying, you know, we'll do some research on job descriptions. As someone who has worked at many organizations that have job descriptions, they have this whole list of things that you do, and then at the bottom it will say, you know, other duties as assigned, and you think, okay, well, this is great. This is what my job will be, and then you go to work for them, and you find out your job is really all other duties as assigned. So you can think this is, you know, what you're going to be doing, but until you actually talk to someone in the field and really get a sense of what reality is, that's your best way to do the research because then you'll really know. And I would talk to more than one person because, obviously, you could talk to someone who hates what they do, and they're going to give you a different picture than someone who doesn't. The great thing about the Internet, of course, is that's a way for you to connect with people in various occupations. And so you might want to try to, you know, hook up with people that way. And just that, you know, I'm just asking you questions about your career and how you got here. Most people are really kind of excited to talk about themselves and, you know, their work and the fact that someone would be interested in them. And so you'll usually get some good information that way. And then just sort of general reading and research about trends that are going on that might lead to possible job opportunities. Just kind of thinking about, well, you know, where could I go? College is another source of information. There are not that many schools, frankly, that have, you know, degrees or certificates in lasers and photonics. It's growing. I mean, I see that it's growing. But there aren't a huge number of schools that have those kinds of programs. But they can be another source of information. And also professional associations. You know, there's like an association for optical engineers and for photonics, careers in photonics, things like that, you know, contacting professional associations frequently. They will have information as well. And I imagine they're very eager to share that information. Yeah. I mean, they want to bring people into the... That's what part of their job is. Oh, yeah. To get that information out there. Exactly. And sometimes if it's not actually handed to you, you do have to take the first step. That's right. And at least request the information. Right. I mean, I think once you get the information, then... Sorry. No, go ahead. Once you get the information, then you really have to go back and say, okay, well, how does this match with what I want to do? I've mentioned a couple of plans in our... Discussion here, the idea of work values. And that's something a lot of people do not think about. They think, yeah, I'm interested in this. Yeah, I would be good at this. But they don't think about how it fits in with the rest of their lives. How... When we talk about work values, what we're talking about is no matter what job I have, what's important to me. What's important to you, Frank, is that you can float around in the pool answering the phone. Right? Yeah. That is very important. That's right. I know. That's a work value for you, having that freedom and that flexibility. So that's something to think about is what are my work values? Could... You know, what are the priorities for me in my life? If making a lot of money, which is a priority for a lot of people, is a primary work value, then you probably need to think twice about pursuing the artistic aspect of holography. Not that you couldn't make money. But I think it would be a lot more difficult to be really rich just focusing strictly on that as opposed to, you know, being an engineer or something. So... Really thinking about what are the things that are important to me? What are priorities for me? How does this work? How does this job fit in with the things that are really important? And that is a key part of the decision-making process because I think a lot of people don't think about that. So I'm sorry. I had interrupted you. No. You interrupted and made some very good points, so I'm happy that you did. And I'm sure so are the listeners. Are you still there? Yeah, right. Just teasing. I know. Okay. The last group, which is probably, I wouldn't say not as important because... Well, the reason I would say that is because they already have jobs. They're professional holographers. So they're already out there. They're getting a check for doing holography each week. Now, all the holograms that you see out there, someone has to produce them, whether it's in a retail store of holograms, some puppy, or a security hologram on a package, or a hologram... I mean, they're already there, but is there anything that you could say to them that could... Yeah. Okay. Just go ahead. Okay. And let me do that. Okay. And this holds true for anyone who is currently in a job or in a career. I don't care what field it's in. I think it's a good idea to periodically... Re-evaluate where you are in your life, and I'll tell you why. A couple of years ago, I was very unhappy in my life in general. So I sat down and created for myself...

A couple of years ago, I was very unhappy in my life in general. So I sat down and created for myself a mission statement, which, you know, some people are cringing because that's just, you know, so corporate. But what I really wanted to do was look at what are the things that are important to me? How do I want to use my talents? What gives me fulfillment? What gives me satisfaction? So I wrote this mission statement, and I talked about, you know, what are the things that I find really satisfying about work? And then I looked at the work that I was doing, and it didn't match. And it hadn't occurred to me prior to that that work was really what was making me unhappy, you know, in my life. I just was going, and, yeah, okay, this is fine. If I hadn't done that reevaluation, I wouldn't have realized, you know, what was going on. So not just because this is how I feel, but this is part of the whole career development process.
